q.q: What is computational thinking?
o: Another name for writing program code in a high-level language
A way of approaching a problem so that a computer can help to solve it
The process of translating source code into machine code
A method of testing a finished program with normal, boundary and erroneous data
q.why: Computational thinking is a problem-solving approach, not the same thing as programming.

q.q: What is decomposition?
o: Removing or hiding the details that are not needed to solve a problem
Breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems
Spotting similarities between problems so solutions can be reused
Writing the steps of a solution as a flowchart or pseudocode
q.why: Decomposition breaks a problem down. Removing detail is abstraction; similarities are pattern recognition.

q.q: What is abstraction?
o: Removing or hiding the details that are not needed to solve the problem
Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved separately
Combining the solutions to several sub-problems into one program
Writing a precise, step-by-step solution to a problem
q.why: Abstraction removes unnecessary detail so you can focus on what matters.

q.q: A Translink route map shows the stops and lines but not every building on the street. Which concept does this show?
o: Decomposition
Abstraction
Pattern recognition
Iteration
q.why: Leaving out details that are not needed is abstraction.

q.q: A canteen ordering app stores each item's name, price and allergens, but not the cook's name. Which concept has been applied?
o: Abstraction, because details not needed to solve the problem have been left out
Decomposition, because the menu has been split into separate items
Abstraction, because the problem has been broken into smaller modules
Decomposition, because unnecessary data has been removed
q.why: Leaving out the cook's name is abstraction. The third option gives the right term with the definition of decomposition.

q.q: Designers of a school canteen app split the job into "show menu", "take order", "take payment" and "print receipt". Which concept is this?
o: Abstraction
Encapsulation
Decomposition
Pattern recognition
q.why: Splitting the problem into sub-problems is decomposition.

q.q: Which is a benefit of decomposition?
o: The program will need no testing once it is finished
Different programmers can work on different parts at the same time
Fewer data items need to be stored by the program
Logic errors are removed automatically from each part
q.why: Separate modules can be shared across a team, tested on their own and reused.

q.q: Which is a benefit of abstraction?
o: The problem is simpler, so there is less data to store and less code to write
Team members can each work on a separate module in parallel
Each module can be tested on its own before being combined
Modules can be reused in other programs without changes
q.why: Abstraction reduces complexity. The other three are benefits of decomposition.

q.q: Breaking a problem down level by level from the main task, often drawn as a structure diagram, is called what?
o: Abstraction
Stepwise testing
Pattern recognition
Top-down design
q.why: Top-down design is decomposition shown level by level, often as a structure diagram.

q.q: Computational thinking is usually described as four elements. Which list gives all four?
o: Decomposition, abstraction, compilation, testing
Sequence, selection, iteration, abstraction
Abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, decomposition
Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithm design
q.why: The four elements are decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithm design.

q.q: In a 6-mark question on abstraction and decomposition, what must be given for each concept to reach the top level?
o: A definition and a second definition worded differently
A flowchart and a pseudocode version of the same example
A definition, an example in the context of the question, and a benefit
An example from a different context to show wider knowledge
q.why: Answers that only define the terms stay in the lowest level; add a contextual example and a benefit.

q.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A precise, step-by-step set of instructions that solves a problem
A program written in a particular high-level language such as C#
A diagram that shows how a problem is broken into modules
The machine code produced when a program is compiled
q.why: An algorithm is independent of any programming language and is designed before coding.

q.q: Which three constructs is every algorithm built from?
o: Sequence, selection and iteration
Input, process and storage
Decomposition, abstraction and iteration
Variables, constants and arrays
q.why: Sequence, selection and iteration are the building blocks of every algorithm.

q.q: Which flowchart symbol is used for a decision?
o: Parallelogram
Rounded rectangle
Diamond
Rectangle
q.why: Decisions are diamonds with one way in and two labelled exits.

q.q: Which flowchart symbol is used for INPUT and OUTPUT?
o: Rectangle
Diamond
Rectangle with double side lines
Parallelogram
q.why: Input/output uses a parallelogram. A rectangle is a process.

q.q: In a flowchart, total ← total + mark should be drawn in which symbol?
o: A rectangle, because it is a process
A parallelogram, because it outputs a total
A diamond, because the total changes
A rounded rectangle, because it ends the loop
q.why: Calculations and assignments are processes, drawn in rectangles. Do not put a calculation in a parallelogram.

q.q: Which flowchart symbol shows that a printed report is produced?
o: Parallelogram (input/output)
Rectangle with a wavy bottom edge (document)
Rectangle with double side lines (subroutine)
Rounded rectangle (terminator)
q.why: The document symbol has a wavy base. The parallelogram is general input/output.

q.q: Which flowchart symbol is used to call a predefined procedure or function?
o: Rectangle with a wavy bottom edge
Rectangle with double side lines
Diamond with two exits
Parallelogram
q.why: The subroutine symbol is a rectangle with double side lines.

q.q: In a flowchart, a flow line goes back from a decision to an earlier step. Which construct does this show?
o: Sequence
Selection
Abstraction
Iteration
q.why: Looping back repeats steps, which is iteration.

q.q: What is pseudocode?
o: Machine code that has been converted back into English
Structured English-like statements that describe an algorithm, independent of any language
A program in C# that still contains syntax errors
A flowchart that has had all its symbols replaced by text boxes
q.why: Pseudocode uses programming keywords but ignores exact syntax, so it converts easily into any language.

q.q: Why is pseudocode useful when designing an algorithm?
o: It can be run directly by the processor, so it can be tested quickly
The designer can concentrate on the logic without worrying about the exact syntax of a language
It is checked by the compiler, so syntax errors are found
It shows the flow of the algorithm as a diagram
q.why: Pseudocode ignores language syntax, letting the designer focus on the logic.

q.q:
total ← 0
FOR count ← 1 TO 5
 INPUT miles
 total ← total + miles
NEXT count
km ← total * 1.609
The inputs are 4, 6, 5, 3 and 2. What value does total hold after the loop?
q.why: 4 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 20. 32.18 is km, worked out after the loop.

q.q: Which statement about pseudocode on this course is correct?
o: Only pseudocode that uses ← for assignment is accepted by CCEA
There is no single official pseudocode; any clear, consistent style earns the marks
Pseudocode must use lower-case keywords such as end if, or it loses marks
Pseudocode must follow C# syntax exactly, including semicolons
q.why: CCEA accepts any clear, consistent pseudocode; ← or = are both fine.

q.q: In a bubble sort, what is compared at each step?
o: The first and last items
The middle item and the target
Two adjacent items
Each item with the smallest item
q.why: Neighbours are compared and swapped if they are in the wrong order.

q.q: In an ascending bubble sort, where is the largest item after the first pass?
o: In its final position at the start of the list
In the middle of the list
Still in its original position
In its final position at the end of the list
q.why: The largest item 'bubbles' to the end during the first pass.

q.q: How does a bubble sort know the list is sorted?
o: Exactly one pass has been completed
The first item is the smallest
The middle item has been found
A complete pass makes no swaps
q.why: No swaps in a whole pass means every pair is in order.

q.q: After pass 1 of an ascending bubble sort on 7, 2, 9, 4, 1, what is the list?
q.why: 7 and 2 swap; 7 and 9 stay; 9 swaps with 4 then 1, so 9 bubbles to the end.

q.q: After pass 1 of an ascending bubble sort on 5, 3, 8, 1, 4, what is the list?
q.why: 5/3 swap; 5/8 stay; 8/1 swap; 8/4 swap, giving 3, 5, 1, 4, 8. The last option is the result after pass 2.

q.q: What is the most passes a bubble sort needs for a list of n items?
o: n
n²
q.why: Each pass places one item; after n − 1 passes the last item must also be in place.

q.q: Why does a bubble sort need a temporary variable when exchanging two items?
o: It counts how many swaps have been made in the pass
It stores the largest value found so far in the pass
It records whether the list is already sorted
Without it, one of the two values would be overwritten and lost
q.why: temp holds one value while the other is copied over it.

q.q: What does a modified bubble sort add to the basic version?
o: A second list that stores the sorted items, so the original is not changed
A Boolean flag that records whether any swap happened, so it can stop when a pass makes none
A search for the smallest item, which is swapped to the front each pass
A counter that limits the sort to exactly n − 1 passes every time
q.why: The flag lets the sort stop early, saving time on nearly sorted data.

q.q: Doubling the length of a list sorted with a bubble sort roughly does what to the time taken?
o: Doubles it
Quadruples it
Halves it
Leaves it the same
q.why: Bubble sort takes about n²/2 comparisons, so doubling n roughly quadruples the work.

q.q: What is a stable sort?
o: One that never crashes, whatever data it is given
One that keeps items with equal values in their original order
One that always makes the same number of passes
One that uses no extra memory beyond the original array
q.why: Stability means equal items keep their original order. Working in the original array is about memory.

q.q: Which is NOT normally used to evaluate a sorting algorithm?
o: The programming language it is written in
The number of comparisons it makes
The number of exchanges it makes
The memory it uses
q.why: Sorts are evaluated on speed, comparisons, exchanges, memory, stability and adaptiveness.

q.q: Which is an advantage of the bubble sort?
o: It is the fastest sort for very large lists of data
It is simple to code and sorts in place, so it needs almost no extra memory
It makes fewer comparisons than an insertion sort on average
It only ever needs one pass to sort any list
q.why: Bubble sort is simple and memory-efficient, but slow on large lists.

q.q: How does an insertion sort begin?
o: It finds the smallest item and swaps it to the front
It compares the first and last items and swaps them if needed
It finds the middle item and splits the list into two halves
It treats the first item on its own as a sorted list
q.why: The first item alone counts as sorted; each following item is then inserted.

q.q: What does an insertion sort do with each new item?
o: Swaps it with its neighbour if they are in the wrong order, then moves on
Compares it with the middle item and discards half the list
Inserts it into its correct place in the sorted part, shifting larger items one place right
Moves it to the end of the list if it is the largest so far
q.why: Larger items in the sorted part shift right to make a gap for the new item.

q.q: An insertion sort on 24 | 11 30 8 19 15 has inserted 11. What is the list after 30 is inserted?
q.why: 30 is larger than 24, so it stays at the end of the sorted part.

q.q: An insertion sort on 5 3 8 1 4 has reached 3 5 8 | 1 4. What is the list after the next item is inserted?
q.why: 1 is smaller than 8, 5 and 3, which all shift right, so 1 goes to the front.

q.q: An algorithm searches the unsorted part for the smallest item and swaps it to the front each time. What kind of sort is this?
o: A selection sort
An insertion sort
A bubble sort
A binary sort
q.why: That is a selection sort, even if printed under another name. Insertion sort takes the next item and shifts larger items right.

q.q: On which data does an insertion sort perform best?
o: Data that is already nearly sorted
Data in reverse order
Random data with no duplicates
Data with an even number of items
q.why: On nearly sorted data each new item needs only one or two comparisons.

q.q: On average, how many comparisons does an insertion sort make compared with a bubble sort?
o: About twice as many
Exactly the same number
About half as many
About a quarter as many
q.why: Insertion averages about n²/4 against about n²/2 for bubble, so roughly half.

q.q: Which statement comparing the bubble sort and the insertion sort is correct?
o: Bubble sort needs extra memory, but insertion sort sorts in place
Insertion sort is unstable, but bubble sort is stable
Both sort in place and are stable, but insertion usually makes fewer comparisons
Bubble sort is faster on large lists, but insertion sort is faster on small ones
q.why: Both are in place and stable; insertion is usually more efficient.

q.q: Sorting the six values 24 11 30 8 19 15, a bubble sort made 14 comparisons in 4 passes. How many did the insertion sort make?
q.why: The notes show 12 comparisons for insertion against 14 for bubble on this list.

q.q: Why is an insertion sort described as adaptive?
o: It changes to a bubble sort when the list is large
It adapts the amount of memory it uses to the list size
It speeds up when the data is already nearly in order
It can sort into ascending or descending order
q.why: Adaptiveness means faster on nearly sorted data.

q.q: In an extended answer comparing the two sorts, what must be included to reach the top level?
o: A comparison of the two sorts only, as descriptions earn no marks
A step-by-step description of each method, then a comparison of efficiency and simplicity
A description of one sort in detail, with the other one named only
A list of other sorting algorithms such as merge sort and quick sort
q.why: A comparison with no description cannot reach the top level.

q.q: What does a linear search do?
o: Checks the middle item and discards half of the list each time
Sorts the list and then checks the first item
Checks the first and last items, then moves inwards
Checks each item in turn from the start until the target is found or the list ends
q.why: Linear means one after another, from the first item.

q.q: When does a linear search stop?
o: When the target is found or the end of the list is reached
Only when the end of the list is reached
After it has checked half of the list
When it reaches an item larger than the target
q.why: A complete description mentions both stopping conditions.

q.q: What is the maximum number of comparisons a linear search makes on 500 items?
q.why: In the worst case (target last or missing) every item is checked.

q.q: On average, about how many attempts does a linear search need for a list of 20 items?
q.why: On average it checks about half the items. 5 is the most a binary search would need.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a linear search?
o: It works on unsorted data and is simple to code
It needs at most 10 comparisons for 1000 items
It is the fastest search for very large lists
It discards half of the list after each comparison
q.why: Linear search works on any list. The other options describe binary search.

q.q: What is the purpose of the found flag in a linear search?
o: It counts how many items have been checked so far
It stores the position of the target in the list
It records whether the list has been sorted
It becomes TRUE when the target is found, so the loop stops straight away
q.why: The Boolean flag stops the loop as soon as the target is found.

q.q: A linear search is written as FOR i ← 1 TO n − 1. What problem does this cause?
o: The first item (index 0) is never checked, so a target stored there is reported as not found
The last item is never checked, so a target stored there is reported as not found
The loop never ends, because i never reaches n
Every item is checked twice, so the search takes twice as long
q.why: Indexes start at 0, so starting at 1 misses the first item.

q.q:
found ← FALSE
position ← 0
WHILE found = FALSE AND position < LENGTH(list)
 IF list[position] = target THEN found ← TRUE
 ELSE position ← position + 1
END WHILE
The list is 14, 9, 22, 7 and the target is 22. What is position when the loop ends?
q.why: Positions 0 (14) and 1 (9) fail; position 2 holds 22, so found becomes TRUE with position 2.

q.q: In the worst case, when does a linear search check every item?
o: When the target is the first item in the list
When the target is the last item or is not in the list
When the list is already sorted into ascending order
When the target appears more than once in the list
q.why: The worst case is target last or missing.

q.q: A shop has an unsorted list of 50 product codes and wants to check whether one code is in it. Which search can be used without first changing the list?
o: Linear search, because it works on unsorted data
Binary search, because it is faster on any list
Binary search, because 50 is an even number of items
Linear search, because it discards half the list each time
q.why: Binary search needs sorted data; linear search does not.

q.q: What must be true before a binary search can be used?
o: The list must contain no duplicates
The list must have an even number of items
The list must be sorted
The target must be in the list
q.why: Binary search relies on order to discard half the list.

q.q: Which item does a binary search check first?
o: The first item
The middle item
The last item
The largest item
q.why: It checks the middle item and discards the half that cannot contain the target.

q.q: In an ascending list, a binary search finds that the target is smaller than the middle item. What happens next?
o: The middle item and everything below it are discarded
The middle item and everything above it are discarded
Both halves are searched, starting with the lower half
The search moves to the next item along and checks it
q.why: If the target is smaller, it must be in the lower half.

q.q: A pupil writes: "A binary search splits the list into two and searches both halves." What is wrong?
o: It splits the list into three parts, not two
It searches the upper half first and then the lower half
Nothing is wrong; this is a correct description
It discards one half every time; that is why it is fast
q.why: Binary search discards one half each time; it never searches both.

q.q: In a binary search for 12 in 3 8 12 19 27 31 40, which item is checked first?
q.why: Seven items have positions 0 to 6; the middle is position 3, value 19.

q.q: In a binary search for 12 in 3 8 12 19 27 31 40, which item is checked second?
q.why: 12 < 19, so last becomes 2; the new middle is position 1, value 8.

q.q: A binary search looks for 40 in 3 8 12 19 27 31 40 52 61 77 using mid ← first + (last − first) DIV 2. Which items are checked, in order?
q.why: mid = 4 (27): first = 5; mid = 7 (52): last = 6; mid = 5 (31): first = 6; mid = 6 (40): found.

q.q: About how many comparisons does a binary search need at most for 1000 sorted items?
q.why: 2¹⁰ = 1024, so about 10 halvings.

q.q: What is the most attempts a binary search can need to find an item in a sorted list of 20?
q.why: 20 → 10 → 5 → 2 → 1 is four halvings, so at most 5 comparisons. 10 is the linear search average.

q.q: In a binary search, what is the search space?
o: The amount of memory the list takes up
The number of items that have already been discarded
The gap between the target and the middle item
The part of the list still being searched, from first to last
q.why: Each comparison halves the search space.

q.q: In a binary search, what does it mean when first becomes greater than last?
o: The target has been found at position first
The list was not sorted, so the search must restart
The search must now continue in the upper half
The search space is empty, so the target is not in the list
q.why: If first passes last, there are no items left: not found.

q.q: Which statement comparing linear and binary search is correct?
o: Linear search is faster on large lists but needs sorted data
Binary search works on unsorted data and is simpler to code
Both searches need about the same number of comparisons on 1000 items
Binary search is much faster on large lists but needs sorted data and is harder to code
q.why: For 1000 items binary needs at most 10 comparisons against up to 1000 for linear.

q.q: What is meant by refining a design?
o: Improving it in stages, after testing and feedback, before it is coded
Translating it into machine code so it can run
Drawing it again neatly as a flowchart
Removing all comments from the algorithm
q.why: Refinement is iterative improvement of a design.

q.q: Why is it better to find a problem during design than after coding?
o: Problems found in the design do not need to be recorded
Fixing it in the design costs minutes; fixing it after the program is in use costs far more
Problems cannot be found at all once the program has been coded
The compiler will refuse to translate a design that contains problems
q.why: Errors are cheap to fix at design stage.

q.q: Which is the best way to find a logic error in a design before coding?
o: Compile it and read the error list
Add syntax highlighting
Dry-run it with test values
Show it to the user as a finished program
q.why: A dry run on paper reveals wrong outputs before any code exists.

q.q: A design repeats the same five INPUT statements. What refinement would help most?
o: Add five more variables
Move the inputs to the end
Replace them with a loop
Change them into OUTPUT statements
q.why: Simplify by replacing repetition with iteration.

q.q: The same validation steps appear in two places in a design. What is the best refinement?
o: Delete one copy, as validation is needed only once
Write them out a third time at the end to check the others
Replace them with a single OUTPUT statement
Move them into one subroutine that is called from both places
q.why: Merging into a subroutine makes the code shorter and any later fix is made once.

q.q: What is stepwise refinement?
o: Testing a program one step at a time using breakpoints in the debugger
Writing the detailed code first and then summarising it as a top-level algorithm
Writing the main steps first, then expanding each vague step into its own detailed algorithm until all can be coded
Removing one step at a time from a design until it no longer works
q.why: Stepwise refinement works top-down from main steps to detail.

q.q: What is a wireframe?
o: A diagram showing how a problem is broken into modules
A simple labelled sketch of each screen, shown to the user before anything is built
A trace table showing the value of each variable as the design runs
The network cabling plan for the computers that will run the system
q.why: Wireframes let the user ask for changes to screens before coding.

q.q: How does agile development affect the refinement of a design?
o: The user is involved only at the start, so the design is refined once
The system is built in small sections and the user reviews each one, so the design is refined again and again
The design is fixed before coding begins and never changed
The programmer refines the design alone, without any user feedback
q.why: In agile development the user reviews each section; in traditional development they are mostly involved at the start.

q.q: Which is the best answer to "Explain how this design could be refined"?
o: Add validation to the design
Make the design better by improving it
Test the design more carefully
Add a range check on age so impossible values are rejected before the price is calculated
q.why: Give a specific improvement and why it helps.

q.q: What do data requirements list?
o: Every screen of the user interface, with its layout and colours
Every test the program must pass, with expected and actual results
Every input, processed or stored value and output, with its name, data type, example and validation
Every subroutine in the program, with its parameters and return value
q.why: Data requirements describe every item of data the solution uses.

q.q: What is a data dictionary?
o: A table recording each data item's name, data type, sample data, purpose and validation
A list of the keywords allowed in a programming language
A file that stores the meanings of every variable name in English
A record of every user of the system and their password
q.why: The data requirements table is often called a data dictionary.

q.q: In a campsite booking system, which data type is best for numNights?
o: Real
String
Integer
Boolean
q.why: Nights are whole numbers, so integer with a range check of 1 to 14.

q.q: In a campsite booking system, pitchSize can only be S, M or L. Which data type and validation fit best?
o: String, with a range check of 1 to 3
Character, with a lookup check for S, M or L
Integer, with a length check of 1
Boolean, with a presence check
q.why: A single letter is a character, and a lookup check allows only S, M or L.

q.q: In a campsite booking system, which data type suits equipment (whether equipment is hired)?
o: Character
String
Boolean
Integer
q.why: Equipment is either hired or not, so Boolean.

q.q: In a data dictionary, why is totalCost marked as "calculated, not input"?
o: It is worked out by the program from other data, so the user never types it
It is a constant that never changes while the program runs
It is typed by the user but not validated
It is input from a file rather than the keyboard
q.why: totalCost is an output calculated from the inputs and the cost per night.

q.q: What is a benefit of working out data requirements before coding?
o: The program will be smaller because fewer variables are used
The user interface can be built without asking the user anything
Testing is no longer needed, as all data has been checked
Every variable gets the right data type and validation is planned rather than bolted on
q.why: Planning data first gives correct types and planned validation.

q.q: Which interface feature stops a user typing an invalid pitch size?
o: A drop-down list of the allowed sizes
A longer prompt explaining the sizes
A larger font for the input box
A label beside the output
q.why: With a drop-down the user can only pick a valid option.

q.q: Which is the most helpful error message for an age of 140?
o: Error 140: invalid data entered.
Invalid input. Program will now close.
Age must be from 0 to 120. Please re-enter.
Error. Please try again later.
q.why: A helpful message explains what went wrong and how to fix it.

q.q: Which is the best prompt for entering an arrival date?
o: Enter date:
Date of arrival please
Arrival date (dd/mm/yyyy):
Input data:
q.why: A clear prompt says what to enter and in what format.

q.q: Which is a strength of a text-based interface compared with a GUI?
o: It is easier for new users to learn
It stops users typing invalid data
It is simple and quick to build and uses little memory
It gives a better user experience
q.why: Text interfaces are simple and small; GUIs are easier to learn and prevent errors with controls.

q.q: Why is consistency important in a user interface?
o: It makes every screen look completely different, so the user always knows which screen they are on
It means the same data is entered twice to check it is correct
It allows the program to run on any operating system
Colours, icons and buttons appear the same and in the same place, so the user learns the system quickly
q.why: Consistency means things look the same and are in the same place on every screen.

q.q: What is a dry run?
o: Working through an algorithm by hand, one line at a time, recording the value of every variable
Running a program on a computer with no input data
Compiling a program to check it has no syntax errors
Testing a finished program on the end user's own computer
q.why: A dry run is done by hand, without a computer.

q.q: Which type of error is a dry run best at finding?
o: Syntax errors
Hardware faults
Spelling errors in comments
Logic errors
q.why: Logic errors give wrong results, which a trace exposes.

q.q: Which columns should a trace table have?
o: Test number, test data, expected result and actual result
Data item, data type, sample data and validation
Pass number, list after the pass and number of swaps
Line, one column for each variable, condition, and output
q.why: A trace table records line, variables, condition and output.

q.q:
x ← 3
WHILE x < 30
 x ← x * 3
END WHILE
OUTPUT x
What is output?
q.why: 3 → 9 → 27 → 81; 81 < 30 is false, so 81 is output. 27 is the common 'stopped one step too early' slip.

q.q: How many lines does for (int i = 2; i <= 10; i += 2) print?
q.why: i takes the values 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10.

q.q: What is output by: for (int i = 5; i < 8; i++) { Console.WriteLine(i * 3); }
q.why: i is 5, 6, 7 (the loop stops before 8), so 15, 18 and 21.

q.q:
total ← 0
FOR n ← 1 TO 4
 total ← total + n
NEXT n
OUTPUT total
What is output?
q.why: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. 6 misses the last time round; 15 adds 5 as well.

q.q: An outer loop runs 3 times and contains an inner loop that runs 2 times. How many times does the body of the inner loop run?
q.why: The inner loop runs completely for each value of the outer loop: 3 × 2 = 6.

q.q: In the youth club age check, valid starts FALSE and the loop runs WHILE valid = FALSE. The inputs are 25 and then 14. How many times is the message "Age must be 11 to 18" output?
o: Once
Twice
Never
Three times
q.why: 25 fails the check, so the message is output once; 14 passes and valid becomes TRUE.

q.q: A pupil is asked how a dry run helps a programmer and writes only "it finds errors". How could the answer be improved?
o: Say that it finds syntax errors as well as logic errors
Make two separate points, e.g. it finds logic errors and it checks the expected output is produced
Say that it is done on a computer, so it is faster than testing
Add that it removes the need for any testing after coding
q.why: Examiners noted many answers made only one point; give two distinct benefits.

q.q: When completing a trace table for a WHILE loop, which slip is most common?
o: Stopping the loop one step too early by not recording the final false test
Recording the condition every time it is tested
Writing a new row for each line executed
Numbering every line of the pseudocode
q.why: Write the condition and its true/false value every time, including the last false test.
